title: Return a boolean, let the caller decide
idea: return vs print: for a yes/no, returning True/False lets an if act on it; printing 'yes' is just text a human reads.

exercises.prompt: You want an if to react to whether a number is even. Which is more useful?
exercises.explanation: Returning True/False lets an if decide. Printing 'even' is just a message — the if can't use it.
is_even(8) returns True, so the if runs and prints yes. The returned boolean drove the decision.

exercises.prompt: A returned True/False can be used as the condition of an if; a printed 'yes' cannot.
exercises.explanation: Right. The if needs a real True/False value. A printed word is just text on the screen.

exercises.prompt: Why let the CALLER decide what to do with the yes/no, instead of printing inside the sub-plan?
options: Different callers may want different reactions to the same answer
exercises.explanation: One caller might print 'yes', another might count it, another might stop a loop. Returning the boolean keeps all options open.
n >= 10 is True for 10 and up. Returning the comparison hands back the yes/no.

exercises.prompt:
Predict:

def big_enough(n):
    return n >= 10

print(big_enough(4))
exercises.explanation: 4 >= 10 is False, so the sub-plan hands back False and print shows False.

exercises.prompt: REVIEW: a comparison like n >= 10 evaluates to...
exercises.explanation: Comparisons produce True or False — exactly the kind of value an if uses and a sub-plan can return.

exercises.prompt: Returning a boolean and then using it in an if keeps the 'decide' job and the 'react' job separate.
exercises.explanation: Yes. The sub-plan decides (returns True/False); the caller reacts (acts on it). Separating jobs keeps code reusable.

exercises.prompt: A sub-plan that prints 'pass' or 'fail' instead of returning True/False is harder to reuse because...
options: the caller can't easily act on the result — it's just text
exercises.explanation: Text on screen can't drive an if or be counted. A returned boolean can. Return the answer; let the caller show it if needed.

options: Return a yes/no so the caller can decide; don't lock it into a printed word
an if can use printed text
exercises.explanation: Returning True/False keeps the decision reusable. The caller can print it, count it, or branch on it.
